idiom_name: java.nio ServerSocketChannel + Selector OP_ACCEPT; Netty ServerBootstrap (boss/worker); Jetty ServerConnector
implementation_notes: Java NIO supplies the primitives — ServerSocketChannel.bind().accept() registered for OP_ACCEPT on a Selector — but the full role split with handler pipelines is framework territory: Netty's ServerBootstrap separates the boss group (accept threads, typically 1) from the worker group (per-connection I/O, scale with CPU cores). Jetty names the acceptor explicitly (ServerConnector). Blocking java.net.ServerSocket with a thread per connection is the manual variant. Netty boss/worker sizing: boss threads = 1-2 (listen sockets are rarely the bottleneck); worker threads = 2× CPU cores for I/O-heavy work, or use an EventExecutorGroup. Configure SO_BACKLOG and SO_REUSEADDR on the ServerSocketChannel before binding.
pitfalls: accept() on a non-blocking channel returns null; act only on OP_ACCEPT readiness.
An accepted SocketChannel starts in blocking mode even when the server channel is non-blocking — configure explicitly.
Thread-per-connection discards the scalability benefit the pattern exists for.
Boss group oversizing causes unnecessary context switches; 1 boss thread per listen socket is almost always sufficient.
Handler pipeline ordering matters; codec (decoder/encoder) must precede application handlers.
